study.title: Acts 15 - the council of Jerusalem and the firmness of the churches
study.overview: Acts 15 tells of a decisive crisis in the early church: some wanted to demand circumcision and observance of the Law of Moses as a condition for the salvation of the Gentiles. The church's answer was to listen to the apostles, to discern God's action among the Gentiles, and to affirm that salvation is by the grace of the Lord Jesus, not by a ceremonial yoke. The chapter also shows how the unity of the church was preserved through consultation, letter, reliable witnesses and pastoral encouragement, and ends with the separation between Paul and Barnabas and Paul's new missionary advancement with Silas.

outline.title: The Controversy on Circumcision and Law
outline.explanation: Some Christians coming from Judea taught that the Gentiles needed to be circumcised and keep the Law of Moses to be saved. The church of Antioch responded by sending Paul, Barnabas and others to Jerusalem to officially deal with the issue, while the outbound path already served to announce the conversion of the Gentiles and to rejoice the brethren.

outline.title: Peter defends the grace of God
outline.explanation: The apostles and elders meet to consider the matter, and Peter recalls that God had already approved the Gentiles by giving them the Holy Spirit and purifying their hearts by faith. He concludes that imposing this yoke would be to tempt God and contradicts the truth that Jews and Gentiles are saved by the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ.

outline.title: James interprets the Scriptures and proposes a pastoral path
outline.explanation: Barnabas and Paul report the signs that God did among the Gentiles, and James connects this to the testimony of the prophets, stating that God is forming for his name a people from among the nations. Their decision is that the converted Gentiles are not disturbed, but receive practical guidance related to idolatry, blood and sexual immorality, in view of coexistence with the Jewish community where the Law was read regularly.

outline.title: The letter, consolation and the new mission
outline.explanation: The church sends Judas and Silas with a letter that rejects the requirement imposed by false teachers and confirms that the decision was made in accordance with the Holy Spirit. In Antioch, the reading of the letter produces joy and consolation; then Paul and Barnabas remain teaching, plan a new visit to the churches and end up separating because of Mark. Still, the work continues: Paul leaves with Silas and travels through Syria and Cilicia, establishing the churches.

study.context: The chapter shows a church still in the early stages, dealing with the entrance of Gentiles and the attempt of some believers of Jewish origin to impose circumcision as a requirement for salvation. The text also indicates the existence of synagogues in various cities, where the Law of Moses was read regularly, which helps explain why the issue had real weight for converted Jews and Gentiles.
study.theology: Acts 15 teaches that salvation is by the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, not by works of the Law, nor by identity rites such as circumcision. The work of the Holy Spirit among the Gentiles acts as a divine testimony of their acceptance, even before any ceremonial imposition. The chapter also shows that apostolic authority does not act in an isolated way: the church discerns in communion, with serious debate, listening to missionary experiences and submission to Scripture. James reads the mission to the Gentiles as fulfillment of God's old plan, which preserves continuity between the prophetic revelation and the expansion of the church. At the same time, Christian freedom is not moral leave: the letter asks for separation from idolatry and sexual immorality, showing that grace saves without making holiness irrelevant.

scholarViews.insight: The men coming from Judea were Jewish Christians who taught the need for circumcision and thereby incorporating Judaism, so that the Gentiles might be saved; the center of the matter was how to receive them in Christian communion.
The council is described as a meeting made by consensus to carefully consider the matter, without hasty judgment, and with the participation of priests with the apostles.
James appears as the one who gives the final judgment of the council; the note points out that he presides over the assembly and that the others discuss or opin, while he pronounces the decision.

questions: Why did the church not accept circumcision as salvation, even though it is a central sign in the history of Israel?
How does the testimony of the Holy Spirit among the Gentiles help to discern the will of God in doctrinal disputes?
How can the church maintain doctrinal unity without erasing real conflicts between brothers and leaders?
study.practice: This chapter calls today's church to discern doctrine with biblical humility, without transforming traditions or cultural marks into a condition of salvation. It also invites us to value decisions made in communion, with listening, clarity and fidelity to the gospel. In practice, it is appropriate to examine whether our demands for other Christians are commandments of God or only our customs; and at the same time, remember that the grace that saves us also calls us to abandon idolatry and sexual sin. Finally, the text encourages strengthening new churches with teaching, encouragement and pastoral accompaniment, as Paul did when visiting the churches again.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not explain in detail the exact relationship between the prohibitions of 15:20 and 15:29 and the coexistence between Jewish and Gentile believers; therefore, the application of these guidelines is presented with caution. There is also not enough basis in the notes to safely state additional historical details about date, exact location of the council or later development beyond what the chapter and the comments inform.
